newsitem.title: ALBANIA: At least 22 die in apparent Albanian looting blast.
newsitem.headline: At least 22 die in apparent Albanian looting blast.

text.p: An explosion ripped through an underground Albanian military weapons store outside Tirana on Wednesday, killing at least 22 people in what police said was probably a looting that went wrong.

The Albanian news agency ATA said the death toll from the explosion close to the town of Burrel, 95 km (60 miles) northeast of Tirana, could rise as many witnesses reported that their relatives had been in the tunnels at the time.
"All the people that were inside the store at the time were killed," a government spokesman said.
Albanian state television reported that a huge fire engulfed two underground tunnels and destroyed many camp buildings.

ATA quoted police as saying the blast was probably caused by gunpowder ignited accidentally in the underground store by looters seeking artillery shells, whose brass casings have created a brisk trade in Europe's poorest nation.

ATA reported that a fire had started at an arms depot in the village of Palikesht, about 120 km (75 miles) south of Tirana, on Tuesday as locals tried to break open artillery shells to steal the casings. No one was injured in that incident.
Police and rescue officials were rushed to Burrel, a chrome mining centre in the central Albanian mountains.
Albanian television reported that the blast took place on Tuesday evening. But the Albanian army Chief of Staff, General Adem Copani, told Reuters it happened early on Wednesday morning.

The weapons store at Burrel was underground like many in Albania, where the former Stalinist leader Enver Hoxha created a huge national arsenal during his 46-year rule, fearing invasion of his isolationist state.

Many of Albania's 1,500 military arsenals were looted last month by people angered at the loss of savings when pyramid schemes collapsed. Unofficial estimates say that up to a million arms have been distributed among the 3.4 million population.

The nine-party government of national reconciliation formed in March to halt the slide towards anarchy is trying to rebuild the army, many of whose members fled as unrest swept the Balkan nation, but it remains well under strength.
Police report that frequent raids on arsenals continue as villagers stockpile arms.
Twenty people were injured last week when an arms store in the northern disrict of Lezhe exploded as youths tried to steal explosives.
Several hundred people have been killed in Albania since the unrest broke out at the end of February, many of them victims of accidental or revenge shootings.
Nearly 6,000 troops from an eight-nation Italian-led force have arrived in Albania in the past two weeks to secure the delivery of humanitarian aid.

The terms of the three-month United Nations mandate for the force allow the troops to secure airports, ports, roads and railways, but do not allow them to disarm Albanians or to act as a police force.
